q1: SELECT O1.SEAT_ID FROM CINEMA O1 WHERE O1.FREE = 1 AND ((SELECT FREE FROM CINEMA O2 WHERE O2.SEAT_ID = O1.SEAT_ID - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT FREE FROM CINEMA O2 WHERE O2.SEAT_ID = O1.SEAT_ID + 1) = 1)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT(C1.SEAT_ID) FROM CINEMA C1 INNER JOIN CINEMA C2 ON C1.SEAT_ID+1=C2.SEAT_ID OR C2.SEAT_ID=C1.SEAT_ID-1 WHERE C1.FREE=1 AND C2.FREE=1
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT O1.SEAT_ID FROM CINEMA O1 WHERE O1.FREE = 1 AND ((SELECT FREE FROM CINEMA O2 WHERE O2.SEAT_ID = O1.SEAT_ID - 1) = 1 OR (SELECT FREE FROM CINEMA O2 WHERE O2.SEAT_ID = O1.SEAT_ID + 1) = 1)
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT DISTINCT(C1.SEAT_ID) FROM CINEMA C1 INNER JOIN CINEMA C2 ON C1.SEAT_ID+1=C2.SEAT_ID OR C2.SEAT_ID=C1.SEAT_ID-1 WHERE C1.FREE=1 AND C2.FREE=1
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent. Q1 selects SEAT_ID from CINEMA where FREE = 1 and at least one of the adjacent seats (SEAT_ID - 1 or SEAT_ID + 1) is also FREE. Q2 joins the CINEMA table with itself on adjacent seats and requires both seats (C1 and C2) to be FREE. This means Q2 returns pairs of adjacent free seats, while Q1 returns individual seats that have at least one adjacent free seat. They can return different results.
counterexample_dsp: A test case where only one seat is free and its adjacent seat is also free. Q1 returns the seat, while Q2 returns both seats. Another case where only one seat is free, but no adjacent seat is free. Q1 returns nothing, while Q2 also returns nothing. A more distinguishing case is when two adjacent seats are free. Q1 returns both seats, Q2 returns both seats as pairs (but only one pair).
